analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income and estate taxes with a single 17% flat tax on wages and business income.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in April 2009, referred to the Finance Committee, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have wiped out the current income tax code and replaced it with a single 17% tax on wages, retirement income, and business profits, with no special rates or brackets. It would also abolish the estate tax, every tax credit (including the child tax credit and the earned income tax credit for working families), and the alternative minimum tax. Investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest would not be taxed at all — only paychecks. Finally, it would lock itself in: changing the rate or creating any new tax benefit later would require a three-fifths supermajority of Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest gains would go to households with high investment income and large estates: capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances would be taxed at zero, and the estate tax would disappear. Business owners would gain from a flat 17% business tax replacing the corporate code. Most workers would see simplified filing, but because all tax credits — including the child tax credit and earned income tax credit — would be repealed, many low- and middle-income working families would pay more while the wealthiest pay far less.

how_it_helps.text: It would replace all individual income tax brackets with a single 17% rate applied to wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction, ending tax filing complexity for most workers.
It would repeal the alternative minimum tax, which currently reaches many middle-income households.
It would tax all business income at the same 17% flat rate regardless of business form, and tax employer-provided benefits like health insurance at 17%.
It would constitutionally-entrench-style lock in the low flat rate by barring future legislation that raises any tax rate or creates any credit unless three-fifths of Congress agrees.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall mainly on wage earners: the only taxable income would be wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation, while income from wealth (capital gains, dividends, interest) would go untaxed. Low-income families would lose the earned income tax credit and child tax credit, which currently make their tax bills negative. Repealing the estate tax removes the only federal levy on large inherited wealth.

drawbacks.text: The tax would fall only on wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation — the earnings of salaried workers — while capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances would be taxed at nothing at all.
It repeals all income tax credits, wiping out the child tax credit and earned income tax credit that lift millions of working families' incomes, replacing them with only a standard deduction.
Repealing the estate and gift taxes entirely removes the only federal tax on very large inherited wealth.
It repeals pension nondiscrimination and minimum-coverage rules, allowing employer retirement plans to be skewed toward executives, and lets employers pull money out of pension plans without penalty.
Its self-locking rule would require a three-fifths supermajority of Congress ever to raise a tax rate or create a new credit, making future democratic adjustment of the tax code very difficult.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification promise is real: a 17% flat tax with a large standard deduction would end filing complexity for wage earners. But the cost side is heavy: it repeals every tax credit that low- and middle-income families rely on (child tax credit, EITC), exempts all capital gains, dividends, and interest from tax, and eliminates the estate tax — shifting a substantial share of the overall tax burden from high-wealth households to wage earners. The flat rate is only revenue-neutral in name; the base narrowing means either fewer public services or higher taxes on salaries relative to wealth. The self-locking supermajority rule would make repairing these effects nearly impossible.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never acted on it: it went to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, drew no cosponsors, and died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Shelby introduced the bill on April 30, 2009; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete, since nothing happened; the existing progressive tax code, which taxes high earners more, simply remained in place. The bill's absence of cosponsors even among Republicans shows the flat-tax proposal had little constituency in the Senate at the time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply expired

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Introduced the flat-tax bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of any party, so no bloc of either party ever lined up for or against it on the record.

industries.industry: High-wealth households and heirs to large estates
industries.note: Investment income of every kind — capital gains, dividends, interest — would be taxed at zero, and the estate and gift taxes would be repealed entirely.
All business income would be taxed at a flat 17% with no corporate minimum tax, AMT, or most credits — a large cut for profitable firms, paid for by a broad base that taxes employer benefits.
They would lose the child tax credit, earned income tax credit, and other credits, while investment income would go untaxed, shifting the tax burden toward wages.

Repeal of nondiscrimination, contribution-limit, and distribution rules plus penalty-free reversion of excess pension assets frees employers from constraints, but the 17% tax on employer-provided noncash benefits like health insurance is a new cost.
A flat tax with one deduction and no credits would eliminate most of the business built on preparing individual returns and advising on credits and AMT.
